analysis.one_liner: Bans BPA from baby bottles, cups, baby food, and infant formula containers.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 7 cosponsors, the bill was sent to the Senate health committee in January 2011 and never received a committee or floor vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have declared food containers for children three and younger, baby bottles, sippy cups, and infant formula containers illegal if they contained bisphenol A (BPA), a chemical used in hard plastics and can linings. It also directed the Health and Human Services Secretary to complete a new safety assessment of BPA in all food containers by the end of 2012, weighing low-dose exposure risks for pregnant women, infants, and children. The bill never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with infants and young children, and pregnant women, who would face less BPA exposure from baby bottle and sippy cup plastic, baby food jar linings, and infant formula cans. States could keep or adopt stricter BPA rules than the federal standard.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it illegal to sell food for children three or younger, baby bottles, or sippy cups in containers made with bisphenol A, with the baby food and formula container bans taking effect 12 to 18 months after passage.

Requires the HHS Secretary to issue a revised safety assessment for BPA in food containers by December 2012, considering low-dose exposure and effects on vulnerable groups including pregnant women, infants, children, and the elderly.
Preserves the right of states, localities, and tribes to adopt stricter BPA rules or require warnings, so the federal standard would be a floor rather than a ceiling.

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers of BPA and of BPA-based epoxy can linings, plus baby food, infant formula, and baby product makers who would need to switch packaging within roughly a year and a half of passage; any added packaging costs could be passed to shoppers.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs would fall on canning and packaging operations that relied on BPA epoxy linings, and some of that cost could reach grocery prices for canned food and infant formula.

The scientific case for harm from low-dose BPA exposure was contested, so critics could argue the ban required industry spending on a risk not yet proven; supporters countered by requiring the new safety assessment to weigh exactly those low-dose effects before any broader rule.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct protections cover a narrow group of products but reach the people most exposed to BPA: babies fed from bottles, sippy cups, and formula cans. The bill's phase-in periods (180 days to 18 months) gave packagers time to switch, and its requirement to safety-test BPA substitutes guarded against swapping one risky chemical for another. The main cost is reformulation spending spread across the food and packaging supply chain.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent the bill to its Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee in January 2011, and it sat there without a hearing or vote for the rest of the two-year Congress.

narrative.text: Senator Dianne Feinstein introduced the Ban Poisonous Additives Act of 2011 on January 25, 2011, with original cosponsors including Senators Schumer, Kerry, Sanders, and Franken.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the day it was introduced.
The bill attracted 7 cosponsors (6 Democrats and 1 independent) and received no further committee or floor action before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers of BPA and BPA-based food container linings avoided a federal mandate to phase the chemical out of baby products, and the committee never had to take a position on the bill.

for.name: Sen. Dianne Feinstein
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to ban BPA from baby bottles, cups, baby food containers, and infant formula containers.

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as an original cosponsor.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee (chaired by Sen. Tom Harkin)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on January 25, 2011 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it during the Congress.

against.name: American Chemistry Council and BPA producers
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against federal and state BPA bans during this period, arguing the chemical was safe at typical exposure levels.

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor was a Democrat or the chamber's independent, Bernie Sanders; no Republican cosponsor appears in the record, and no vote was ever taken to test broader support.

industries.note: The bill would have phased BPA out of baby bottles, cups, and food and formula container linings, cutting a major market for the chemical. The industry had a record of fighting similar bans, and its interest in continuing sales ran against the bill's child-health goal.

industries.industry: Food canning and packaging (baby food and infant formula)
industries.note: Canners would have had to replace BPA epoxy linings within 12 to 18 months, bearing reformulation costs that could reach grocery prices. Nothing in the bill blocked packagers from selling safe products, and many had already begun moving away from BPA.

Makers of polycarbonate bottles and cups would have lost a product line, but several major brands had already removed BPA in response to consumer demand, so the ban largely ratifies a shift already underway rather than forcing a costly reversal.
